title: The bowl of oil
hook: carry a full bowl of oil past a crowd and a dancing beauty, a swordsman behind you (SN 47.20)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the gatekeeper, and your line was the same. When a mood arrived, did you name it before you let it in? Day three hundred ninety-one.

A huge crowd is gathering in the town square. Word has spread: the most beautiful woman in the land is here, and she's dancing and singing. People are pushing to see. Now a man is handed a bowl filled to the very brim with oil, and told to carry it straight through the middle of all that, between the crowd and the dancer. Behind him walks another man, with a drawn sword. Spill one drop, he's told, and you lose your head. Today: the bowl of oil.
screen: `THE CROWD PUSHES TO SEE.` → `A BOWL FULL TO THE BRIM.` → `A DRAWN SWORD BEHIND.`

segments.voice: The Buddha tells this at Sedaka, the same town as the acrobats. And he asks his monks a simple question. Would that man stop paying attention to the bowl, and let his eyes drift to the dancer? No, sir, they say. Of course not. Then the Buddha says what the picture means. The bowl of oil filled to the brim stands for mindfulness of the body. So train yourselves, he says, to develop mindfulness of the body, to make it your vehicle and your ground. The picture is extreme on purpose, and each piece is worth a look. The crowd and the dancer are everything that pulls attention outward: the alerts, the drama, the bright, loud, lovely things. The sutta doesn't explain the sword, but one way to read it is as the seriousness of the stakes. Not that distraction is a crime; just that it may cost more than we tend to think. And the bowl is the body itself: the breath, the feet, the hands, right here. Not something far away. The thing you're already carrying. Notice what the man doesn't do. He doesn't shut his eyes. He doesn't stay home. He walks straight through the crowd while the music plays. The practice isn't avoiding life. It's carrying something steady through the middle of it. That's right mindfulness at its most physical. Attention isn't floating somewhere up in the head. It's in your hands, at the brim of the bowl, step by step, while everything around you invites you to look away.
screen: `WOULD HE LOOK AWAY?` · `THE BOWL: MINDFULNESS OF THE BODY.` · `THE SWORD: THE STAKES ARE REAL.` · `THROUGH THE CROWD, NOT AROUND IT.` · then, large: `DON'T SPILL.`

segments.voice: If you can, fill a cup or glass with water, right to the top, and hold it. If not, imagine one in your hands. Feel its weight. Now, slowly, carry it a few steps, or simply raise it and lower it, without spilling. Notice how the whole body gathers around the brim: the breath slows, the hands soften, the eyes stay close. That's the bowl of oil. Then set it down and sit, feeling the same steadiness in the body. The bell holds the time.
The bowl of oil. The Buddha's image for mindfulness of the body: carried brim-full through the crowd, without spilling.
Your line: don't spill. Today, carry one full cup slowly, through your kitchen or your office, and let the rest of the room wait. Day three hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: Many Buddhists practice mindfulness of the body in walking meditation and daily tasks, and some teachers have students carry a full cup or bowl slowly as a training in steady attention.

fork.setup: you're carrying a bowl of oil full to the brim. the crowd roars: the dancer has started. a man with a sword walks behind you. what do you do?
options: glance at the dancer, just once.
keep your attention on the bowl.
set the bowl down and watch.
fork.reveal: the monks answer that the man wouldn't neglect the bowl for a moment; the Buddha says the bowl is mindfulness of the body.

original.note: Pali kāyagatā sati: mindfulness directed to the body, which the brim-full bowl stands for.

trapdoor: what you thought: mindfulness is a mental exercise.
what it means: attention held in the body, carried steady through the middle of ordinary life.
what a scholar hears: SN 47.20 calls the brim-full bowl a designation for kāyagatā sati, and the dancer is the janapadakalyāṇī, 'the beauty of the land'.

notes: SN 47.20 paraphrased (at Sedaka among the Sumbhas; crowd and the beauty of the land dancing and singing; bowl of oil full to the brim; man with drawn sword; the bowl as kāyagatā sati). Confirm.
Woodward's 1930 Kindred Sayings V translation was not quoted.

The sutta glosses only the bowl (kāyagatā sati); the readings of the crowd, dancer and sword in the teach and games are interpretive, and the sword line was softened in review. Confirm a Keeper is comfortable with them.
The 'carry a full cup' practice in howItsDone is a common teaching exercise; phrased as 'some teachers'.
